Chapter Seven: On Receiving and Maintaining.
Regarding the explanation of this chapter, there are briefly two points: first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the formal explanation of the text. Explanation [of the Title].
Regarding the title of this chapter: according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is called "receiving" (*udgrahaṇa*) because one hears and practices [the teaching] by the power of faith;
it is called "retaining" (*dhāraṇā*) because one does not lose it for a long time by the power of mindfulness.
This chapter precisely elucidates how the thirteen Dharma masters uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and further cause others to uphold it; thus, it is titled the "Chapter on Upholding.

Second, one sees that the Buddha Bao-man (Treasure-Filled) upon the platform is the master of the emanations of all Buddhas; according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, this is Vairocana Buddha—also called Lúzhāonà or Lúzhēluó, which translates as "Illumination"—because the pure form of the Reward-Buddha pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, the light of the sun, moon, and lamps pervades a single location; this is also one with Rocana.
Alternatively, its name may be translated according to its meaning as "Jewel-Full" (Ratnapūrṇa).
This Buddha manifests as the thousand-petaled Śākyamuni Buddha and the transformation Buddhas upon the ten billion petals; therefore, he is called the Lord of Transformation Bodies.

Regarding the third manifestation of a thousand-petaled lotus world above the Buddha: this refers to the thousand Buddhas upon those thousand petals, as well as the ten billion Buddhas upon each individual petal.
Among them, each of the aforementioned Buddhas individually expounds the Prajñāpāramitā.
This corresponds to what is said in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: "I, now as Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal."
Upon the thousand petals surrounding [the central one], there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis.
On each petal are ten billion lands, and in each land is a Śākyamuni; each sits beneath a Bodhi tree, attaining the Way of Buddhahood simultaneously.

This is the first [stage].
The Sūtra says:
"The Bodhisattva of the nature of the stage of cultivation."
The commentary states:
From here below, the thirteen Dharma masters are explained individually in sequential order, divided into thirteen sections.
This is the first: the explanation of the *śikṣāgotra* (the nature of training).
The textual divisions are fivefold:

first, the designation of the stages and enumeration of their names; second, the differentiation of their categories; third, the distinctions among their activities; fourth, the elevation of the inferior to reveal the superior; and fifth, the temporal duration of entering the stages.
This is the first section, which establishes the positions and lists the names.
That is to say, among the thirteen types of Dharma masters, the first Dharma master is named the Bodhisattva of the Nature of the Cultivated Seed (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*).
The Sūtra says:
"If [a layperson] goes to a bhikṣuṇī":
the commentary explains that this second [section] distinguishes the different categories.
A brief explanation of the fourfold assembly:
first, the *upāsaka*; second, the *upāsikā*; third, the *bhikṣu*; and fourth, the *bhikṣuṇī*.
Regarding the term *upāsaka*, it is sometimes called *upāsa*; both are corruptions or abbreviations.
"Uposaka" is correctly translated as "lay male devotee" (jinsi nan);
"upāsikā" is translated as "lay female devotee" (jinsi nü).
"Saka" is the masculine form, while "sikā" is the feminine form.
This means that because they constantly attend upon and serve virtuous persons, they are called *upāsaka* (lay followers); the detailed explanation is as before.
As for the *bhikṣu* and *bhikṣuṇī*, they are also explained as before.
Sūtra: One practices the ten wholesome actions.
Commentary:
Third, the differences in their practices.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the cultivation of the ten wholesome actions; second, the cultivation of impurity and patience; and third, dwelling within the Buddha-family.
This refers to the cultivation of the ten wholesome deeds, namely the ten paths of wholesome karma such as non-killing, or alternatively, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Although there are two interpretations regarding these ten types of faith, the intention of the *Benji* (Original Record) lies with the ten stages of faith.
Sūtra: One contemplates one's own body, down to its individual parts, as impure.
Commentary:
Second, the cultivation of the patience regarding impurity has three aspects:
first, contemplating the impurity of the six elements; second, contemplating the impurity of the sense organs; and third, contemplating the impurity of the three realms.
This is the contemplation of the six elements, meaning that the bodies of all sentient beings are composed of the six constituents:

namely, the four great elements, the space element, and the contaminated consciousness element of the form realm. Because these are all contaminated and subject to destruction, they are termed "impure."
Because one contemplates the six elements individually, it is said that they are "divided part by part.
The Sūtra states:
"Furthermore, one contemplates the fourteen faculties up to the bodhicitta."
The commentary states:
Second, the impurity of the faculties (*indriya*).
This refers to further contemplating fourteen of the twenty-two faculties as being impure.

The so-called five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, together with the five consciousnesses, may be included within the category of sentient beings and are thus called the five faculties of sensation (*pañca-vedanendriya*).
The five faculties of feeling consist of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity;
along with the male, female, mind, and life faculties, these fourteen are all tainted (*sāsrava*) and possess immeasurable faults; therefore, they are all said to be impure.

The five faculties beginning with faith and the three untainted faculties are all exclusively of a wholesome nature; since they are not mentioned beyond this point, the practitioner of contemplation contemplates these fourteen faculties, thereby giving rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Sūtra: One constantly cultivates the gate of contemplation leading up to the stage of patience within the three realms. Commentary:
Third, one contemplates the impurity of the three realms.
This means that because all phenomena bound to the three realms are with outflows (sāsrava), they are also impure. Question:
The four dhyānas and the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) also possess pure phenomena (śubhadharma); how then can they be said to be impure?
The explanation states:
impurity itself has many varieties.
As stated in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are six kinds of impurity:
first, the impurity of putridity, which itself has two types.
The first is internal impurity, referring to hair, body hair, and so forth.
Second is impurity based on the external, namely the bluish discoloration and so forth.
Second is the impurity of suffering and affliction, namely the sensations produced by painful contact.
Third is the impurity of inferiority, namely the desire realm.
Fourth is impurity by way of relative dependence (*apekṣā-aśubhatā*): for example, in relation to the superior purity of formless phenomena, the various phenomena of the form realm appear as impure;
and in relation to the nirvāṇa that is the cessation of the personal aggregate (*pudgala-kāya*), everything up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) appears as impure.

Fifth is the impurity of afflictions (*kleśāśubhatā*), which refers to all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) within the three realms.

Sixth is the impurity of disintegration (*vipariṇāmāśubhatā*), which refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); they are impermanent, non-eternal, unreliable, and by their very nature subject to transformation and decay, as explained in detail therein.
Because of this, these dhyānas and formless attainments are all termed "impure.
The Sūtra says:
"Dwelling in the family of the Buddha."
The commentary states:
Third, abiding in the family of the Buddhas.
This section has two parts:
The first part clarifies dwelling in the Buddha’s family, while the latter part explains the cultivation of the six points of respectful harmony.
This refers to the former.
That is to say, emptiness and non-self are the dwelling place of the Buddha, and are thus called the "Buddha’s family."
This stage of the nature of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) is called "abiding" because one first realizes the principle of emptiness.
The Sūtra states:
"Cultivate the six points of respectful harmony up to the path of the perfections (*pāramitā*)."
The commentary states:
Second, the cultivation of the six points of harmonious respect.
This means that because one dwells in the household of the Buddha, one cultivates the six points of harmonious respect.
What are called the three karmas, shared precepts, shared views, and shared study of the eighty-four thousand pāramitās constitute the six points of reverent harmony.

"Good son, [this practice] has both decline and progress."

This refers to Bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten faiths prior to the practice of patience (*kṣānti*); because they may regress or advance, it is called the "inferior position.

First, by practicing the ten right paths for ten thousand kalpas and generating the bodhicitta, one shall enter the stage of *śikṣā-kṣānti*.
Third, one also constantly studies the three levels of *kṣānti* (forbearance).

It means that at the beginning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one first realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); because by this realization one attains the nature of a noble being (*ārya-gotra*), one is called a "person of certainty" (*niyata-pudgala*) and is also non-retrogressive.

Commentary:
Second, the abandonment of transgressions has four levels:
first, not committing the five heinous crimes, namely: killing one’s father or mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

Second, the non-arising of the six grave offenses, as explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, "Chapter on Receiving Precepts": first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, selling intoxicants; and sixth, slandering the fourfold assembly of both lay and ordained followers.
The detailed exposition is as found in other sutras, where it is said that there are four grave offenses or eight grave offenses.
As for the four grave offenses: first, covetousness and envy; second, stinginess; third, anger; and fourth, slandering the Triple Gem and its treasury.

Regarding the "eight grave offenses," these refer to the eight grave offenses of a bodhisattva; by adding the four grave offenses of the Saṃgha to the previous four, they are termed the eight grave offenses.
Regarding the "ten grave offenses," by adding the four [offenses] such as greed to the previous six, they are termed the ten grave offenses.
Now, these six offenses that cause one to lose the dharma of precepts upon their commission are called "heavy dharmas" (*guru-dharma*).
They are termed "heavy" because they exceed all others in gravity.

Third, there are twenty-eight minor offenses that must not be committed, as also explained in the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, "Chapter on Receiving Precepts": first, failing to make offerings to one's parents, teachers, and elders;
Second, being addicted to and delighting in drinking alcohol;
third, being defiled and evil such that one cannot attend to those suffering from illness;
fourth, seeing beggars but being unable to give according to one's means, whether much or little, and instead sending them away empty-handed.
Fifth, if upon seeing bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, elders, seniors, or various upāsakas and upāsikās, one fails to rise to welcome them, pay homage, or inquire after their well-being;

sixth, if upon seeing bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have violated the precepts they received, one gives rise to arrogance in the mind, saying, "I am superior to them; they are not my equal";
seventh, if during the course of a month one cannot observe the eight precepts for six days and make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Eighth, there was a place for preaching the Dharma forty *li* away that he could not go to hear;
ninth, he accepted bedding and seats belonging to the *caitya-saṃgha*;
tenth, suspecting that there were insects in the water, he nevertheless drank it.
Eleventh, traveling alone without a companion through dangerous and perilous places;
twelfth, staying overnight alone in a nunnery;
thirteenth, beating, scolding, or mistreating one's slaves, servants, or outsiders for the sake of wealth or one's own life.
Fourteenth, if one gives leftover food to a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā;
fifteenth, if one keeps cats or wildcats;

sixteenth, if one keeps and raises elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, or donkeys—any such domestic animals that have not been rendered pure—and gives them to those who have not received the precepts;
Seventeenth, if one does not store the *saṃghāṭī* robe, the alms bowl, or the mendicant’s staff;
eighteenth, if for the sake of one’s own life one must engage in agricultural work, one should not seek out impure water or land unsuitable for planting;

nineteenth, for the sake of one’s own life, if one engages in trade by weighing goods with bushels or scales, once the price has been stated, one must not subsequently renege on it to shift from the cheap to the expensive; when measuring goods with bushels or scales, one must not manipulate them before or after the transaction; if they are unequal, one should speak up to have them made equal.
Twenty: engaging in sexual desire at an improper place or time;
twenty-one: carrying goods for sale and failing to pay official taxes while stealing and deceiving others;
twenty-two: violating the laws of the state.
23. If one obtains new grain, fruits, melons, or vegetables and consumes them first for oneself without first offering them to the teacher or making offerings to the Triple Gem;
24. If one preaches the Dharma or offers praise when the Sangha has not authorized it;
25. If one walks on a path ahead of the bhikṣus or ahead of the śrāmaṇeras;
Twenty-sixth: among the monastic community, when food is being distributed, one who selectively chooses the finest portions for their teacher and gives them in excessive measure;
twenty-seventh: one who raises silkworms; twenty-eighth:
while traveling, upon encountering a sick person, failing to stop and provide care or take measures for their benefit, but instead entrusting them to someone else and departing.

The fourth is the dharma of the truth of non-arising, which means that those established in the stage of certainty do not slander the Buddha-dharma by claiming that the scriptures were not spoken by the Buddha.
The Sūtra says:
"One can reach the stage of Saṃghāta through a single asaṃkhyeya-kalpa."
The commentary states:
Fourth is the period of entering the stage.
In the Sanskrit language it is *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, which here is translated as "incalculable eons."
This means that because the number of days, months, and years cannot be counted, it is called *asaṃkhyeya*.
Alternatively, it is so named because the kalpas of the three calamities and so forth cannot be counted.
Furthermore, according to the systems of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the term "three great *asaṃkhyeyas*" refers to the *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpa].
In this context, the calculation is based on the number of days, months, and years, rather than the three calamities and so forth.

Regarding the stage of *saṃghāta*, the traditional commentary explains it as the "nature-lineage" (*gotra*) or "freedom from attachment"; that is, having realized the emptiness of persons, one does not cling to a self, sentient beings, and so forth.
This means that by practicing and cultivating patience for one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one first enters the nature of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*).
As the Sūtra says:
Furthermore, regarding the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*).
The commentary states:
Second, the nature-lineage.
The textual exposition has three parts:
first, the designation of the stages and the enumeration of their names; second, the differentiation of the contemplations; and third, the temporal duration for entering the stages.
This is the first part.
The initial stage of learning is called "cultivation" (*śikṣā*), because through repeated practice it becomes one's nature.
The ten stages of practice (*daśa-pratipatti*) are therefore termed the "nature-lineage" (*gotra-bhūmi*).
The Sūtra says:
"Practicing the contemplation of the ten wisdoms.
The commentary states:
Second, the differentiation of the contemplations is explained.
Within this, there are five parts:

first, the practice of contemplation; second, the elimination of hindrances; third, the knowledge of the conventional; fourth, the refinement of contemplation; and fifth, the cultivation of practice. This is the first.

Regarding the ten wisdom-observations of speech and action, these refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the three roots of goodness, and the observation of the three periods of time, as explained previously in the "Chapter on Teaching and Transforming."
Sūtra: "The cessation of the ten inversions.
Commentary:
Second is the elimination of hindrances.

Regarding the statement "eliminating the ten inversions," this means that the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness eliminates the four inversions; the contemplation of the three roots of goodness eliminates the three poisons; or the contemplation of the three periods of time eliminates attachment to the three periods of time.
The fixed attachment to the existence of past causes, future effects, and present causes-and-effects is all contrary to reason and is termed "perversion.
The Sūtra states:
"From self, person, knowledge, and vision, up to the point where they are unattainable."
The commentary states: Third, the knowledge of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

This refers to the self, the person, and the knower; according to worldly convention, these are merely provisional designations for various parts and lack substantial existence. That which exists only as a name is a "provisional designation of name" (*nāma-prajñapti*); that which exists only as sensation is a "provisional designation of sensation" (*vedanā-prajñapti*); and that which exists only as phenomena is a "provisional designation of phenomena" (*dharma-prajñapti*).
By this principle, [the self] is truly unfindable; therefore, one knows that the "self," "person," and so forth all exist conventionally.
Sūtra: From the absence of fixed characteristics up to the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness.
The commentary states:
Fourth is the cultivation of contemplation.
Regarding "the absence of fixed characteristics," this generally indicates that both the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) lack any fixed characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "because there is no characteristic of self or other," this separately explains that both the self and phenomena lack the characteristics of self and other.
This constitutes two interpretations.
The first says:
The absence of self-characteristics reveals the mark of non-self;
the absence of other-characteristics reveals the mark of non-dharmas.
One interpretation states:
"Absence of self-characteristics" means the absence of the characteristics of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) and a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātman*).
"Absence of other-characteristics" means the absence of the two kinds of "mine" (*mamakāra*) associated with both the personal self and the phenomenal self.

Regarding the cultivation of the gate of protection (*rakṣā-vipaśyanā*): as in the aforementioned gates of contemplation, that which has not yet been attained is called "cultivation," while that which has already been attained is called "protection."
The meaning and intent of the preceding passage are difficult to comprehend.
There are various divergent interpretations, which I fear would be too prolix to recount here.
The Sūtra states:
"Furthermore, one constantly practices a million [recitations] up to every single thought-moment, never departing from them.
The commentary states:
"The fifth is the stage of cultivation."
This means that because contemplation becomes progressively superior in this stage, one practices the various *pāramitās* while never being separated from [the bodhicitta] in mind.
The Sūtra states:
"By means of two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one reaches the stage of *prabhākari*."
The commentary states:
Third is the period of entering the stage (*avasthā*).
Regarding *paritrā*, according to the *Mūla-ṭīkā*, it is translated as "guarding" (*śubharaṇa*).
This refers to the stage of the lineage of the path (*mārga-gotra*), wherein its practice is firm and its intrinsic nature is not lost; this is called the stage of protection (*ārakṣaṇāvasthā*).
This clarifies that by practicing the Dharma of the right path for two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one attains the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).

If one follows the *Benji* (Original Record) in assigning the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to the name "Path-Seed Nature" (*mārgajñatā-gotra*), it would contradict the scriptural teaching that the "Noble Womb of Subduing Patience" (*vinaya-kṣānti-āryagarbha*) consists of thirty persons.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, the Path-Seed Nature..."
The commentary states:
Third is the lineage of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatāgotra*).
This section is divided into three parts:
First, the positions are indicated and their names listed; second, the distinctions among the contemplations are analyzed; third, the timing of entering the stages is discussed.
This is the first [section].
Because it is the lineage of the noble path on the stages (*bhūmi*), it is called the "lineage of the path" (*mārgagotra*).

Therefore, the aforementioned sutra states: "Practicing the supreme patience of subduing (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one enters the path of equality," which is termed the "nature of the path-variety" (*mārga-jñatā-gotra*). The sutra further states:
"Abiding within firm patience (*dṛḍha-kṣānti*), one reaches the state of neither arising nor ceasing."
The commentary states:
Second, the differentiation of the modes of contemplation.
This section contains two parts:
First, the distinctions between the contemplations are analyzed; second, the superiority or inferiority of the retributions received.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:

first, a general indication of the characteristics of the contemplations; second, a detailed exposition of the ten contemplations; and third, the citation of the superior to distinguish it from the inferior.
This is the first stage.
Abiding in the ten firm minds is called "abiding in patience" (*kṣānti*).

This means that in this stage, one contemplates all phenomena as being non-arising; since arising is not established, there is consequently no abiding or ceasing—this is the meaning of contemplating emptiness.
Sūtra: "That which is called the five aggregates of clinging is ultimately unobtainable. Commentary:
Second, the ten contemplations are described individually: namely, the five appropriations, the three realms, and the two truths.

Regarding the "five appropriations," the five outflowing aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that are grasped by craving and other afflictions are called the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādāna-skandha*).
By contemplating that [reality], one attains the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*).
By contemplating the three realms (*traidhātuka*), one attains the three patiences of emptiness (*trividhaśūnyatākṣānti*).
By contemplating the two truths (*satyadvaya*), one attains the two patiences of impermanence and non-arising (*anityānutpādakṣānti*).
As explained extensively before,
these ten dharmas are all said to be empty because they lack the characteristics of self and other, as well as any intrinsic nature, and are thus unapprehendable. Sūtra:
"And constantly entering the ultimate state where the mind is utterly stilled.
The commentary states:
Third, this distinguishes the superior from the inferior by citing excellence.

This means that although one practices the ten types of patience (*kṣānti*) within this stage, when distinguishing them according to their full measure, one sets aside the preceding nine patiences and practices the contemplation of the tenth, the patience of true reality (*satyakṣānti*). This is precisely what is called the contemplation of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*), which is termed the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Regarding "the mind and mind are stilled and extinguished" (*cittacittavyupaśama-nirodha*): "stilling" (*vyupaśama*) means tranquility, and "extinguishing" (*nirodha*) means elimination. That is to say, the mental activities of that very mind are tranquilized moment by moment, and its agitation is eliminated; therefore, it is called "the mind and mind are stilled and extinguished."
Sūtra: And they undergo birth within the three realms.
Commentary:
Second, the superiority and inferiority of the retribution received.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the heading; second, the inquiry; and third, the explanation.
This is the general statement:
although the mind is tranquil, one still undergoes the retributive fruits of birth within the three realms. Sūtra:
Why is this? The commentary states:
the second [point] is an inquiry.
That is to say, an external critic asks:
"Having already attained quiescence, how can one receive the retribution of segmented existence?
The Sūtra says:
"Karmic habituation and karmic retribution reach the arising of the Path of Accordance.
The commentary states:
This is the third, the correct explanation.

This means that by the power of the habitual perfuming of past karma, one undergoes the segmented birth and death within the three realms; because this serves as the basis for the Noble Path, it is called "birth conducive to the Path."

Alternatively, it may be that for the sake of transforming sentient beings, one assumes a body within the six realms of existence; because this accords with the Noble Path, it is called "birth in accordance with the path.
Although there are these two interpretations, the former explanation is superior.
As stated above, because bodhisattvas of the spiritual lineage (gotra) are not born into the evil realms,
the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they reach the state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma)."
The commentary states:
Third is the stage of entering the position (*avasthā*).
The term "equal noble ones" (*sama-ārya*) refers to the stages (*bhūmi*).
This refers to entering the noble path of the first bhūmi, wherein one is free from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped.
Alternatively, it may be said that the first bhūmi simultaneously realizes the two truths; hence, it is called "equality.
*Abhibhūti* (Avinivartanīya) is translated here as "non-retrogression."
This means that from the first bhūmi upward, one realizes the principle and does not regress; this is called "non-regression.
Because one has cultivated the various pāramitās throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one shall enter the stage of the noble ones and abide in non-regression.
Sūtra: Furthermore, O Good Awakening Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Commentary:
Fourth is *Sudṛśa* (Good Perception). This section has five distinct parts:

first, the designation of the stage and the enumeration of its names; second, the differentiation of the cultivation; third, the timing of entry into the *dharmakāya*, beginning with "By means of the four"; fourth, the differentiation of rebirth, beginning with "Without the three realms"; and fifth, the limits of ascending the stage, beginning with "Constantly cultivating."
This is the first section, which marks the positions and lists the names; it may be understood according to what precedes. Sūtra:
Abiding in the patience of equality up to the mind that does not depart.
The commentary states:
Second, the differentiation of the cultivation [of the path].
The text is divided into two parts:
The first part reveals the distinct characteristics of the two wisdoms; the second part, beginning with "In this way, good son," again clarifies their similarities and differences.
Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the establishment of the two chapters; second, the detailed explanation of the two chapters, beginning with "Entering the relinquishment of signlessness."

This is the first [chapter]. Regarding "the patience of equanimity" (*samaropa-kṣānti*): the first chapter clarifies that its ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is free from the marks of existence and non-existence; this is termed the patience of equanimity.

Regarding "practicing the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*) with every thought without departing from the mind": this establishes the second, the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), which refers to transforming sentient beings through the four means of integration; this is termed the wisdom of skillful means.
Sūtra: Entering into signless equanimity leads to the abandonment of the afflictions of craving.
Commentary:
From here below is the second section, the detailed explanation of two chapters.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of true wisdom, which explains the aforementioned equality; [the second follows].
Following the section on "Immeasurable," the subsequent portion reveals the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) and explains the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Within the preceding section, there are three parts:

first, a general indication that true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) extinguishes the greed of the three realms; second, a detailed explanation of how true wisdom realizes the three unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*); and third, the manifestation of how these unconditioned states are free from the marks of existence and non-existence.
This is the first [point].
Because its nature is non-attachment, which abandons the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), it is able to extinguish the afflictions of craving within the three realms.
The Sūtra says:
"In the ultimate sense, it reaches the unconditioned nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The commentary states:
Second, the specific explanation of how true knowledge (*bhūta-jñāna*) realizes the two types of the unconditioned.
The textual exposition is divided into three parts:

first, the unconditioned state of dharmatā; second, the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and third, the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is the first part.
This has two names:
first, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); second, space (*ākāśa*). Sūtra:
"Extinction through reliance on principle reaches the signless and the unconditioned.
The commentary states:
"The second is the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."

This refers to the suchness that is manifested when all characteristics of afflictions and so forth are extinguished through taking suchness as an object; this suchness is the unconditioned state known as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). It has three names:
first, cessation through deliberation.
The essence is itself wisdom (*jñāna*).

"Discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) means analytical discernment (*viveka*); because cessation is attained through such discernment, it is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Second is "cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Number" (saṃkhyā) refers to the mental factor of wisdom (prajñā). That which is attained through the factor of wisdom is called "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The three types of knowledge (jñāna) take cessation as their object; thus, "deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā) and "wisdom" (prajñā) are identical in meaning.
The Sūtra says:
"When abiding in the first patience, one reaches the signless and unconditioned.
The commentary states:
"The third is the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."

This refers to abiding in the first stage of the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) within the stage of receptive faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*); by permanently severing all conceptualized afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*), one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding immeasurable future phenomena—an unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) that is signless (*animitta*).

This has three names: first, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, non-enumerative cessation (*apratyaya-nirodha*); and third, non-wisdom-conditioned cessation (*ajñāna-pratyaya-nirodha*). These should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].

However, regarding the distinction between these two types of cessation, according to the Sarvāstivāda school: that which is attained through the abandonment of hindrances by means of wisdom is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); cessation that does not arise from wisdom is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

According to the Sautrāntika school, the cessation of afflictions through contaminated knowledge is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), while the cessation through uncontaminated knowledge is termed "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, this is largely the same as the Sautrāntika position, as detailed in a separate chapter.
Question:

Since space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not objects of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), how can the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*) realize the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)? Explanation:
[The answer is as follows:]...
The various schools differ in their tenets.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is not permitted for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to take the two unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.
According to the Mahāyāna school, however, because these are provisionally established upon true thusness (*tathatā*), there is no fault in permitting such an object.
Sūtra: "From signlessness and unconditionedness up to the absence of even signlessness.
Commentary:

Third, it reveals that the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence, intending to show that the nature of these three is entirely empty.
However, there are differing interpretations regarding this passage.
One explanation states:
The explanation of signlessness consists of three phrases.
First, "the absence of self and other" eliminates the notion of having signs.
"Non-existence of non-existence" eliminates the mark of non-existence.
By saying "because it is the mark of non-existence," both the marks of existence and non-existence are simultaneously eliminated. Some say:
It fully dispels the four propositions.
Being without the marks of self or other, it dispels the mark of existence.
Being without non-existence, it dispels the mark of non-existence.

Regarding the term "signlessness" (*animitta*), it eliminates the third alternative—the sign of both existence and non-existence—and the fourth alternative—the sign of neither existence nor non-existence.
Now, to explain:
"the absence of self and other" eliminates the mark of a self (*ātman*), thereby revealing the non-existence of the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
"Non-existence of non-characteristic" indicates that the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is not itself without characteristic; therefore, it is said to be "non-existent.
It is not a characteristic of existence, and thus it is called "characteristicless.
The Sūtra says:
"Immeasurable skillful means all manifest before one's observation.
The commentary states:
Second, this reveals the wisdom of skillful means.
The textual analysis has two parts:
first, a general presentation of the six kinds; second, a detailed explanation of the six kinds.
This is the first part.
Furthermore, it is called "immeasurable" because it is not singular, and it is called "expedient means" because it is not the wisdom of internal realization.
The Sūtra states:
"The expedient means of the true mark leads to non-perversion."
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which provides a detailed explanation of the six kinds of skillful means.
This is divided into six parts, each consisting of two sections:
First the summary, then the explanation.
This explains the first [topic]: the skillful means of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
It is called "true nature" because it takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as its object; it is called "skillful means" because it gives rise to skillful functional capacity.
Question:
What is the distinction between this and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*)? Explanation:

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Fundamental wisdom internally realizes the unchanging image of its own essence; subsequent wisdom, however, takes true suchness as its object by perceiving a transformed image, and thus cannot directly realize the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)."
Regarding the terms "not sinking" and so forth, various explanations differ.
According to the *Benji* (Original Record), ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are called "sinking" because they are submerged in birth and death;
those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are called "emerging" because they have emerged from birth and death.

To say that from the thirty minds up to the ten stages they are called "non-retrogressive," while the stage of Buddhahood is called "non-perverted," and that one studies this dharma during the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), is not correct.
Why is this so? That explanation by the Śākya [Vasubandhu] places the aforementioned good sons below the first stage (*bhūmi*);
the subsequent passages belong to the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), which do not accord with the intent of the sutra, and therefore I shall not rely upon them here.
Now, the explanation is as follows:
it is not so. One says:

The first two stages, as described above, can be transformed through the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*); however, the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) still involve inversion.
Since the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is free from the preceding four positions, it is said that there are no four [inversions] therein.
One interpretation states:
"Sinking" (līna) refers to torpor (styāna), which is an obstacle to meditative concentration (samādhi).
"Emergence" (vyutthāna) refers to restlessness (auddhatya), which is an obstacle to wisdom (prajñā).
"Transformation" refers to other afflictions such as doubt.
"Perversion" refers specifically to perversions such as the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is free from the four aforementioned faults; therefore, these four negations are taught.
Sūtra: "Universally training in skillful means until reaching all trainings.
Commentary:
Second, the expedient means of universal study.

According to the *Benji* (Original Record): "Within the conventional there is the real, yet it is not the realization; within the real there is the conventional, yet it is not that realization does not occur."

Some say: "Because it does not include humans, devas, or the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) among the five vehicles, it is not a definitive proof; yet because it does contain the Mahāyāna, it is not a case of failing to prove [the Mahāyāna].
It is like the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, which extensively studied various heterodox doctrines and thoroughly understood the intent of the noble ones."
Furthermore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states that one should study the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and so forth, without discriminating between what is realized and what is not.
Although there is no such distinction of realization or non-realization, one is nonetheless able to study all phenomena.
Some versions state "all training," which is erroneous.
The Sūtra says:
"By means of the skillful means of dedication, one directs [merit] toward sarvajñā (omniscience)."
The commentary states:
Third is the skillful means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
This refers to seeking great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), which differs from the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) that seek to abide in a minor fruit; thus it is called "not abiding in a fruit."
Unlike ordinary beings, they do not seek to abide in the fruits [of the path]; this is called "not non-abiding.
Seeking to advance toward Bodhi is called "heading toward Sarvajñā" (all-knowledge). Sūtra:
"Unshakable by the four māras despite the mastery of Māra.
The commentary states:
Fourth, "the skillful means of mastery over Māra" refers to the skillful means of drawing others in.
Regarding "practicing the Buddha-way through non-ways," this refers to what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Sometimes manifesting as a courtesan to attract those who lust after beauty;
first using the hook of desire to entice them, and later leading them into the Buddha-way."

"Unmoved by Māra" refers to the passage in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "Practicing dhyāna while remaining amidst desires, causing Māra’s mind to become confused and agitated, so that he cannot find an opportunity."
Regarding the four māras: first, the affliction-māra; second, the aggregate-māra; third, the death-māra; and fourth, the celestial-māra.
To these four preceding māras, one adds impermanence, non-self, impurity, and suffering; these are the distinct names for the eight māras.
Another explanation is as follows:
although they perform the deeds of Māra, they possess mastery through skillful means; therefore, this is called "the skillful means of Māra’s mastery.

Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation teach and transform sentient beings through the power of skillful means, manifesting themselves as Māras."
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Buddha-way" states: "If a bodhisattva practices what is not the way, this constitutes penetrating the Buddha-way.
How does a bodhisattva practice what is not the way?
The answer is:

"A bodhisattva practices the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya) without affliction or distress; even to the point of saying: 'He manifests the presence of wives, concubines, and court ladies, yet he is always far removed from the mire of the five desires—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to penetrate the Buddha-way.'"
He recounted it exactly as it was.
The Sūtra says:
"The skillful means of the One Vehicle leads to all practices."
The commentary states:
Fifth is the skillful means of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This means that because the essence of principle is non-dual, it is called the One Vehicle.
Skillfully knowing the distinct characteristics of sentient beings within the Single Vehicle Dharma is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
The phrase "non-dual characteristic" explains the aforementioned Single Vehicle.
The phrase "thoroughly penetrating all modes of practice therein" explains its skillful means.

Furthermore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The dharma-realm is without differentiation; it is for the sake of delivering sentient beings that the three vehicles are taught through differentiation.
Moreover, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Buddhas, by the power of skillful means, differentiate and teach the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle."
The exposition of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is explained in detail as in a separate chapter.
The Sūtra states:
"Through the skillful means of transformation, he reaches the pure Buddha-lands."
The commentary states:
Sixth is the skillful means of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
"Transformation" is another name for "alteration."
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, based on this, speak of "transformative birth-and-death" (*pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa*), which is termed "transformational birth.

This clarifies that bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*)—by virtue of their power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*)—undergo transformative birth within pure lands; they do not receive the segmented bodies (*prātibhinnaka-śarīra*) of the triple world, and thus it is called the "expedient means of transformation."
Sūtra: "In this way, son of good family, up to the illumination of true wisdom.
Commentary:
Second, the re-explanation of the similarities and differences between the two types of wisdom.
This section has three parts: first, a summary of the aforementioned characteristics of difference;
Next, an analogy is raised to clarify that [the dharmakāya] is neither identical to nor different [from the buddha-qualities];
subsequently, the phrase "by the accomplishment of all practices" clarifies the accomplishment of practice.
This is the first [point].
The textual analysis has two parts:
first, the manifestation of the characteristics of ultimate wisdom; second, the manifestation of expedient wisdom.
This is the former.

This means that in the first stage (*bhūmi*), fundamental wisdom arises, and one initially awakens to the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena (*dharma*) and of persons (*pudgala*). Therefore, it is called "initial awakening wisdom.
This very awakening wisdom is non-dual regarding the marks of existence and non-existence; thus, it is the illumination of true wisdom.
Therefore, the preceding passage states: "There is no characteristic of self or other, because there is no absence of characteristics.
Sūtra: Skillful application without realization, up to the contemplation of skillful means.
The commentary states:
Second, the wisdom of skillful means is revealed.
The phrase "skillful application" serves as a general heading for the four types of application.
This refers to the four types of skillful application of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of that very stage, which are termed "skillful application.
Regarding the phrase "not realizing [them as such]," this separately clarifies these four applications.
"Not realizing" means not being like the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who realize the four dhyānas and take them to be *nirvāṇa*.
"Not sinking" means not being submerged in birth and death like ordinary beings.
"Not emerging" means not departing from birth and death like those of the Two Vehicles.
"Not arriving" means not failing to reach the First Ground like Bodhisattvas prior to the grounds.

Alternatively, it may be that "not arriving" (*aprāpta*) is an error; one should instead say "not inverted" (*aviparīta*). This means that because Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) still give rise to inversions, the term "not inverted" is used to distinguish them from those [ordinary beings].
Regarding this contemplation of skillful means, the summary of the four aforementioned functions all constitutes subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
The Sūtra says:
"For example, water and its waves are neither identical nor different."
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which employs analogies to demonstrate that [the relationship] is neither identical nor different.
This text is divided into two parts:

First, it clarifies that the two wisdoms are neither identical nor distinct; subsequently, by analogy, it demonstrates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) likewise have an essence that is neither one nor many.

That is to say, these two aforementioned wisdoms exist within a single moment: they are not identical because their two functions are distinct, yet they are not distinct because they share the same wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is like the waves of water: because their substance and characteristics are distinct, they are not one; yet because the waves are identical to the water, they are not different.
As the Sūtra says:
"Even all modes of practice are neither one nor two."
The commentary states:
Second, the analogy explains that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise neither identical nor different.

That is to say, just as two types of wisdom are neither identical nor different, so it is for everything up to the eighty-four thousand perfections (*pāramitā*), the various gates of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and the gates of dhāraṇī; when compared with one another, they are all neither identical nor different.
Sūtra: "And each and every practice is accomplished.
Commentary:
Third, the accomplishment of practice (*caryā-sampad*).
This means that because two types of wisdom are accomplished within this stage, all other practices are fully accomplished. Sūtra:
"By means of four asaṃkhyeyas, one reaches the gate of the treasury of merit.
The commentary states:
This is the third [stage], the period of entering the treasury.

This means that when untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*) is perfected in this stage, it encompasses all gateways of merit; for this reason, it is established separately as the "Gateway of the Treasury of Merit" (*guṇagarbha-mukha*).
Logically, this gateway should exist in all stages, yet because it is not the first [stage], it is not established separately there.
The intended meaning here is that one enters this treasury-gate by practicing the four *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of various deeds.
Some commentators explain:
according to the preceding and following context, this passage should be placed after all the pure lands have been described.
Why is this? Because when the four kalpas are completed, one shall enter the subsequent stage. Sūtra:
"Because the karma of the three realms has reached its ultimate end, one does not create new [karma].
The commentary states:
Fourth, the distinction regarding the taking of birth.
The textual analysis has two parts:
first, clarifying non-birth within the three realms; second, clarifying birth in the Pure Land.
This is the former.

This means that upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one severs the discriminating view of self and no longer creates karma of the three realms; thus, one exhausts past karma without creating new.
Question:
Since Bodhisattvas on the stages do not receive a body of segmented birth (*prādeśika-śarīra*), by what karma do they receive the retributions of the ten kings as described in various texts?
The masters of the Western regions have two interpretations of their own. One states:
since Bodhisattvas on the stages all undergo transformation (pariṇāmanā), the ten kings they encounter are all transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya).
It is not so; otherwise, the ten sense bases would not perceive the King, for his transformed, wondrous body is not within their domain.
One school says:
There was a master of the treatises named Vinayaprabha who, relying on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, made this statement:
The royal bodies manifested from the eighth stage upward are exclusively transformational;

prior to the seventh stage, one still gives rise to afflictions, which support karma within the three realms to receive a segmented body—this is a substantial body that receives the retribution of the ten kings, and thus there is no error.
Sūtra: "By the power of their vows, they reach all pure lands.
Commentary:
Second, by the power of their vows, they are born in a pure land.
There is an interpretation that this is stated from the perspective of the majority.
If the afflictions act as a sustenance, one may be reborn within the three realms, as stated in the *Tāḍanaprabha-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says:
"Constantly cultivate the contemplation of equanimity until it is constantly bestowed upon others."
The commentary states:
Fifth is the stage of ascending to the position (*pada-pratisthā*).
This section consists of two parts:
The first part clarifies the ascending of the throne; the latter clarifies the bestowal of jewels.
This section clarifies the ascending of the throne of *Kumāra*.
According to the *Benji* (Original Record), it is translated as "Victorious over Māra."
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is free from the five fears, thereby transcending the maras of the two vehicles.
The Sūtra states:
"One constantly bestows the four great treasuries of jewels upon others."
The commentary states:
Second is the gift of jewels;
there are various differing explanations regarding this.
One says: "The Tripiṭaka and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka are bestowed upon all sentient beings.
Another says:
According to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, there are four kinds of precious treasuries:
first, the priceless, which is the Bodhisattvayāna;
second, the high-priced, which is the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
The third is of middling value, which is the Śrāvaka-yāna;
the fourth is of inferior value, which is the human and celestial vehicles (*manuṣya-deva-yāna*).
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) that benefit sentient beings are called the four precious treasuries.
Sūtra: Furthermore, Bodhisattva Guṇamati.
Commentary:
Fifth, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the designation of the stage and the enumeration of names; second, the discernment of the distinctions in contemplation; and third, the temporal duration of entering the stage.
This is the first [point].
It means that when the three types of virtuous discipline, such as the pratimokṣa, arise together with wisdom, it is called "virtuous wisdom" (guṇaprajñā).
The Sūtra says:
"By means of the four immeasurable minds.
The commentary states:

In order to counteract the affliction of hatred (*dveṣa*), one cultivates the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

It extinguishes the afflictions such as anger within the three realms of existence.

Second, this distinguishes the removal of obstacles.
By cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one is able to extinguish afflictions such as hatred within the three realms.
However, regarding the affliction of hatred, there are differing views among the various schools.
According to the Sarvāstivāda, it exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
According to the Sautrāntika school, hatred (*dveṣa*) pervades all three realms.
According to the Mahāyāna school, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, it is the same as the Sarvāstivāda.
Now, following this sutra, it is in agreement with the Sautrāntika explanation.
Alternatively, this sutra follows a method of sequential exposition (*anuvartana-yukti*).

Alternatively, the words here are general while the intended meaning is specific; that is to say, because anger exists within the realm of desire among the three realms of existence, it refers to them as "the three existences."
In terms of actual reality, hatred and the like do not extend to the higher realms.
The Sūtra states:

The commentary states:
Third is the stage of the limit (*avasthā-pramāṇa*).

This refers to the stage of abiding in faith (*śraddhā-vihāra*), which pervades the three stages; since this corresponds to the second [of those], it is called "intermediate patience" (*madhyama-kṣānti*).
This means that in this stage, one universally cultivates all practices, beginning with the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
As the Sūtra says:
"By means of five *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one brings all sentient beings to transformation."

Third is the stage of entering the position (*avasthā-praveśa*).
*Jñānabala*, according to the *Mūla-ṭīkā*, is translated as "the power of fulfillment."

This means that because one practices the contemplation of great loving-kindness throughout five great kalpas such that it is constantly present before one, the power of wisdom becomes perfected for the sake of transforming all sentient beings; thus, one also enters the stage of *śatadharā*, which is also called *viśatadharā* and named "Fearlessness."
Sūtra: Furthermore, regarding the person of clear wisdom. Commentary:
Sixth, the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu.
This section has three parts:
first, the designation of the stage and the naming; second, the analysis of the distinctions in contemplation; and third, the temporal duration for entering the stage.
This is the first stage.
Because one practices the contemplation of the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) within this state, it is called "clear wisdom" (*vidyā-prajñā*).
The Sūtra says:
"Always attaining the three types of clear knowledge through the signless.

Second, the differentiation of the contemplations.
The textual exposition is divided into three parts:
first, the manifestation of the distinct practices of the stages; second, the discernment of the removal of hindrances according to the positions; and third, the clarification of fulfillment.
Within the first part, there are two sections:
First, the three types of clear-knowledge contemplations are indicated; later, their specific characteristics will be explained. This is the first [part].

Regarding the three types of clear-knowledge contemplations: first, the clear knowledge of the recollection of past lives; second, the clear knowledge of death and rebirth; and third, the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. These are explained in detail in the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).
Sūtra: "Knowing the dharmas of the three periods of time leads to the mind's cessation within the mind.
Commentary:
Second, the explanation of its characteristics.
"Knowing the dharmas of the three periods of time" indicates the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).

"Knowing that the dharmas of the three periods of time have no coming, no going, and no place of abiding" specifically reveals the objects traversed by these three types of supernormal knowledge; that is to say, the future has not yet come to be, the past has already ceased, and the present does not abide. This differs from the Sarvāstivāda school, which maintains that all three periods possess substantial reality.
Regarding "the mind and mind are quiescent": because there are no objects of perception (*ālambana*), the perceiving mind is quiescent in every thought-moment.
Sūtra: "Exhausting the delusions and afflictions of the three realms."
The commentary states:
Second, the analysis of the stages and the removal of hindrances.
Because one knows the three periods of time, one is able to eliminate the delusions regarding the three periods of time within the three realms.
Sūtra: "Because one attains the contemplation of all merits through the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā). Commentary:
Third, the fulfillment of clear wisdom (*vidyā*).

This means that because one has eliminated ignorance regarding the three periods of time, one is able to attain the contemplations of the various merits that accord with the three types of clear wisdom (*traividyā*). Sūtra:
"Constantly [employing] six asaṃkhyeyas to reach all dharmas.
Commentary: This is the third stage, the period of entering the position.
*Kāṣṭhā* means "crossing the limit" (*du bian*).
This refers to the stage wherein one is free from all base and inferior views; therefore, it is called *kāṣṭhā*.
Although this interpretation exists, it has not yet been verified against the authentic text.
It is said that because the six great *saṃghas* gather immeasurable light, they enter the stage of *Kārāṭa*, upholding all dharmas through practice free from marks (*animitta*).
Sūtra: Furthermore, [it concerns] the Bodhisattva Āryabodhi. Commentary:
From here below is the seventh [section], the Dharma Master.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the designation of the positions and the listing of names; second, the manifestation of the specific practices of each stage; and third, the temporal duration of the stages and practices.
This is the first [stage].
As for the term "er-yan" (爾炎), it is translated here as "Mother of Wisdom.

This means that within this stage, the two types of emptiness—the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*)—are able to give rise to the Noble Path; therefore, it is called the "Mother of Wisdom."
Regarding the term "sacred awakening and penetration" (*ārya-bodhi-prativedha*): it refers to the noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*) that is produced.

In the first three stages, the practices of giving, morality, and cultivation are identical to those of ordinary beings; however, within this [fourth] stage, one gives rise to the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). At this point, one first realizes sacred awakening and penetrates the principle of the two kinds of emptiness; hence, it is called "sacred awakening and penetration."
Sūtra: One practices the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*). Commentary:
Second, the distinct practices of the stages (*bhūmi*).
This section has three parts:
first, the stage of cultivating the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*); second, the arising of the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and third, the limits for the cessation of hindrances.
Within the first stage, the text further contains two parts:
the first pertains to the Patience in Accordance with Truth (anulomikī kṣānti), and the latter distinguishes the state of abiding. This is the former.
This means that within the stage of "conformity-patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti), there are three levels: inferior, middling, and superior.

This fourth stage occupies the position of the initial patience among these three; because it conforms to the Noble Path, it is called the "cultivation of the patience that accords with the Dharma" (dharmānulomika-kṣānti).
Sūtra: "One who flows against the five views reaches the stage of a Srotāpanna.
Commentary:
Second, the clarification of their stages of abiding.
Regarding the term *srotāpanna*, there are two meanings:
first, "flowing against the current," and second, "cultivation."

In this stage, one gives rise to the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), turns against the current of the five views, and accumulates immeasurable virtues; therefore, it is called "abiding in the stage of Srotāpanna.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, this is translated as "Stream-enterer" (pre-stream).
"Stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*) means "entry"; "stream" refers to the stream-like category. Because one first enters the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*), it is called "stream-entry.
Question:

Since these five views that arise through conceptual discrimination have already been permanently severed upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), how can it be said here that one "goes against the stream of the five views" based on the fourth stage?
The commentary explains:

According to the actual analysis, the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) are abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*). What is abandoned now is their residual habituation (*vāsanā*), which is termed the "abandonment of the five views.

If this were not the case, then doubt—which is subsumed under the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) and is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-heya*)—would [likewise] be abandoned at the first stage; how then could it be said here that it is abandoned in the fifth stage?
Thus we know that this is explained in terms of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The Sūtra says:
"Constantly employing the divine eye up to the supernormal power of the body."
The commentary states:
This refers to the second arising of the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Since one has not yet reached the ultimate state within this stage, the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is excluded from among the six powers.

As for the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and in the following sections that a bodhisattva has exhausted their outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), this is a provisional designation of "exhaustion of outflows" based on a stage where they have not yet fully exhausted them; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Sūtra: "In every moment of thought, one extinguishes all views pertaining to the three realms.
Commentary:
This is the third stage of the elimination of obstacles (*āvaraṇa-pramāṇa*).
That is to say, within this stage, it corresponds to the *srotāpanna*; therefore, it is said that one is able to eliminate all views (*dṛṣṭi*) pertaining to the three realms. Sūtra:
"Also because it does not depart from the mind.

Regarding the stages and periods of practice:

because one practices the five supernormal powers and the *pāramitās* throughout seven great kalpas, within the state of full perfection, the aforementioned merits are never separated from form (*rūpa*).
Sūtra: Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattva Viśeṣagāmin. Commentary:
Next, the eighth category, the Dharma Master, is analyzed.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the designation of the rank and the enumeration of names; second, the manifestation of the specific practices of each stage; and third, the temporal duration of the practice.
This refers to the first [ground].
It is called "superior penetration" (*viśeṣa-adhigama*) because one is able to thoroughly comprehend two or three truths; it is also called "superior wisdom" (*viśeṣa-prajñā*).
Alternatively, on this ground, the ultimate and conventional truths proceed together; since this ground can excel in such a difficult task, it is named "superior penetration."
Sūtra: Regarding the patience that accords with the Path, there are the four fearlessnesses. Commentary:
Second, the manifestation of the specific practices of the stages (*bhūmi*).
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); second, the discernment of the removal of obstacles; and third, the demarcation of the entry into the stages.
Within this enumeration, there are two distinct sections:
first, a general presentation of the four numbers; second, a sequential detailed explanation.
This is the former.

This means that in the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), based on the patient acceptance that accords with the Path (*anulomikī kṣānti*), one gives rise to the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Because the mind is free from timidity or dread regarding the four external challenges, they are called "fearlessnesses.
The Sūtra states:
"One contemplates *nayuta* truths until reaching the state of an All-Knowing One (*sarvajña*)."
The commentary states:
Second, the detailed explanation according to sequence.
The explanation of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) is divided into four parts.
This is the first fearlessness regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*), which means there is nothing unknown regarding two objects.

First, the observation of "many" truths (*nayuta-satya*); that is, the second and third truths, as well as the eight truths, and so forth, whose number is extremely great, is termed "many" (*nayuta*).
The second is the study of the inner path’s treatises, which refers to the *adhyātma-vidyā* (inner science) among the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*).
The treatises of the non-Buddhist paths refer to the *hetu-vidyā* (logic) and *śabda-vidyā* (grammar).
Medical prescriptions refer to the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*).
The mastery of crafts and techniques are all part of the *śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā* (the science of arts and crafts).

Although these four branches of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*) apply to both Buddhist and non-Buddhist systems, for the sake of this context, they are described according to their common characteristics as being "external" [to the Buddhist path].
When I say, "I am the Omniscient One," I proclaim my own title of virtue.
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), each possesses two meanings:
first, there is the arising of doubt due to clinging to traces.
This refers to external challenges and objections: for instance, when the Buddha asks Ānanda from where he has come, or asks what sound an external noise is, etc.
If [the Buddha] possesses all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), why would he pose such questions?
Second, he proclaims his own title of virtue:
"I am the All-Knowing One; it is in accordance with worldly custom that I offer this consolation. Sūtra:
"Having extinguished the three realms up to the complete exhaustion of the mark of self.
The commentary states:
Second is the fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*).
There are also two matters:
first, clinging to the traces gives rise to doubt.
That is to say, an external objection states:

The World-Honored One sometimes spoke with loving words to Rāhu and rebuked Devadatta; how then could his outflows be exhausted? Furthermore, he himself proclaimed his own virtues, saying, "My outflows are already exhausted.
This was done in accordance with worldly conventions to manifest [the appearance of] love or anger. (Some versions read "my marks are already exhausted," which is an error.)
Sūtra: Because one knows that each stage (*bhūmi*) has its own emergence, it is called the "path leading out" (*nairyāṇika-mārga*). Commentary:
Third, the fearlessness of revealing the path to the cessation of suffering also has two aspects:
first, harboring doubts regarding the tracks [of practice].
That is to say, an external opponent objects:
"The various noble paths cannot exhaust suffering,
for we observe that even Arhats still experience sufferings such as being bitten by snakes, which suggests that suffering has not been exhausted."
Second, they proclaim their own virtuous titles.
This means that all Arhats have severed future suffering; therefore, it is said they "sever suffering," not that they say they sever it because present suffering is non-existent.
The Sūtra says:
What is it that does not emerge which is therefore called an obstacle to the Path?
The commentary states:
Fourth, delusion is able to obstruct fearlessness regarding the Path.
There are also two matters:
first, clinging to the traces gives rise to doubt.
This means that although those such as *srotāpannas* possess craving and other afflictions, because they possess the Noble Path, desire cannot obstruct the Path.
Third, he proclaims his own qualities;
while these cannot obstruct the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and so forth, they can obstruct the path to the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and so forth.
Thus far, the four fearlessnesses of the Buddha have been explained.
In this present passage, the fearlessness of the bodhisattva on the fifth stage is explained;
the characteristics of this fearlessness can be understood immediately.
The Sūtra says:
"Reversing doubt regarding the three realms.
The commentary states:
Second, the removal of hindrances.
This is said in terms of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and thus it speaks of "removing doubt.
In reality, however, [doubt] has already been severed, as it consists solely of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The Sūtra states:
"Having cultivated and accumulated immeasurable [merit], one enters the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The commentary states:
This is the third section, the delimitation of the stages of entry.

This means that because within this stage one has already extinguished the delusions such as doubt pertaining to the three realms, and has cultivated and accumulated immeasurable supreme qualities, one thereby enters the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) is here translated as "one who comes and goes once.

This means that having completely severed the six grades of afflictions of the desire realm, because three grades still remain, one returns once more among humans and devas; thus, one is called a "once-returner."
Sūtra: Furthermore, one collects the practice until it reaches the state where the mind does not depart. Commentary:
Third, the period of cultivation:
it refers to the fact that on this stage, one cultivates various *dhāraṇīs* and the four fearlessnesses for eight eons, never allowing them to depart from the mind.
Sūtra: Furthermore, it is eternally manifest as reality.

first, the designation of the position and enumeration of names; second, the discernment of the distinctions in contemplation; and third, the clarification of the duration of practice.

"Abiding within the Patience of Accordance."
